tagline: Sharp curves and surviving masonry trace an early stone turnpike.
intro: Georgetown Pike runs 11.79 miles from Dranesville to Langley, passing through Great Falls and along the edge of Great Falls Park. It begins as a two-lane road, then bends sharply into the valley of Difficult Run. The highway became the first Virginia Byway in 1974 for its scenic value.

Built between 1813 and 1827, the pike had a crowned stone roadbed. Workers used hand tools and horse-drawn equipment to clear, blast and fill the rough terrain, adding retaining walls, culverts and bridges where needed. In 1820, Falls Bridge Turnpike Company president John Mason Jr. reported large fitted stones twelve inches deep at the center, topped with six inches of broken stone. The original route continued to the Potomac at Chain Bridge, beyond today’s SR 193. In 1963, Virginia completed the Dolley Madison Boulevard bypass as an alternative to widening Georgetown Pike and Chain Bridge Road.

Heading east from Leesburg Pike, pass Great Falls’ village center at Walker Road before the curves beside the park and down to Difficult Run. Beyond the Madeira School, the road crosses Bull Neck Run and Scott Run. It widens to four divided lanes at the Capital Beltway interchange in McLean, then passes Langley High School and ends at Dolley Madison Boulevard.

moments.title: Great Falls
moments.text: Great Falls was once known unofficially as Forestville, but another Forestville already had a post office. The community took its present name in 1955 from the nearby falls of the Potomac. Forestville survives in the name of the old school, built in 1889 and enlarged in 1911 by adding the Floris School. After closing as a school in 1922, the building became a residence and later the Great Falls Post Office, from 1959 to 1982. The resulting L-shaped wooden building has weatherboard siding and a metal cross-gable roof. The 1929 Grange Hall is brick, with a front porch supported by concrete pillars.

moments.title: Great Falls Park
moments.text: Great Falls Park preserves remnants of the Patowmack Canal and the canal town of Matildaville beside the Potomac. The canal was designed to carry boats past the river’s rapids. At Great Falls, workers included enslaved people rented from nearby plantations, indentured servants and other laborers. They used black powder to cut through rock for the final three locks. High construction costs and insufficient revenue bankrupted the company. Viewing platforms in the park overlook the falls; the canal remains tell a separate story of attempts to navigate them. The National Park Service took over Great Falls Park in 1966.

moments.title: Difficult Run
moments.text: Georgetown Pike descends through sharp curves into Difficult Run’s valley. The stream’s name came from long-boatmen working in the Patowmack Company era, who found two bends of the Potomac near its mouth treacherous. Road builders faced their own crossing here: John Templeman designed and built a chain bridge to carry the pike over the stream. That bridge no longer survives. Below the road, Difficult Run travels through a narrow, cliff-lined valley before reaching the Potomac. Templeman served as the road’s superintendent from December 1817 through April 1818, bringing experience from building the Potomac Chain Bridge.

moments.title: Bull Neck Run
moments.text: An original road bridge with a stone-and-brick viaduct survives at Bull Neck Run. The pike reaches this crossing after passing the Madeira School on the eastbound drive. Its builders fitted the road to the terrain with stone retaining walls, culverts, arches and bridges.
